result: Kit is an evolutionarily conserved, loss-of-function intolerant proto-oncogene receptor tyrosine kinase (pLI = 0.98, LOEUF = 0.17) that is enriched in specific neuron populations and tentatively associated with rare cases of neurological dysfunction.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are supported by citations to Chen et al., 2022 and Bernstein et al., 1990, and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B. The pLI and LOEUF scores provide quantitative evidence of loss-of-function intolerance, and the association with neurological dysfunction is appropriately described as 'tentative' given the reliance on case reports.

result: Kit mutations result in diverse pleiotropic conditions including pigmentation disorders, hematological disorders, infertility, mastocytosis, and gastrointestinal disorders. Severe global KL-Kit hypomorphs exhibit fatal anemia, and developmental Kit depletion in the cerebrum results in death of neuronal progenitors or nascent neurons.
evaluation: Claims C3, C9, and C10 are supported by citations to review articles (Bernstein et al., 1990; Lennartsson and Rönnstrand, 2012) and primary research (Guijarro et al., 2013; Mashayekhi and Gholizadeh, 2011; Aoki et al., 2017). These claims establish the pleiotropic nature of Kit and provide context for why conditional knockout approaches are necessary.

result: KL and Kit are mutually expressed in discrete connected neuron populations across species and decades. Inactivating Kit mutations have been implicated with CNS disorders including developmental delay, ataxia, hypotonia, intellectual disability, deafness, and autism spectrum disorder. KL-Kit manipulation alters axon outgrowth in vitro and in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C4-C8 are supported by multiple citations spanning several decades (Keshet et al., 1991; Motro et al., 1991; Hirota et al., 1992; Manova et al., 1992; Gore et al., 2008; Su et al., 2013; Guijarro et al., 2013) and case reports (Telfer et al., 1971; Finucane et al., 1991; Funderburk and Crandall, 1974; Lacassie et al., 1977; Kilsby et al., 2013). However, the evidence for neurological dysfunction is limited to case reports, and the axon outgrowth studies are in vitro or developmental, not addressing synaptic function directly.

result: In mice, rats, and humans, Kit is abundantly expressed by molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) of the cerebellar cortex, while cerebellar Kit Ligand is restricted to Purkinje cells (PCs), which receive GABAergic synaptic inhibition from MLIs.
evaluation: Claims C11, C12, C13, C15, and C16 are supported by citations to Motro et al., 1991; Hirota et al., 1992; Manova et al., 1992; Kim et al., 2003, and by Figure 1A and B showing immunohistochemistry data. The expression pattern is well-established in the literature and confirmed by the authors' own data.

result: The authors generated a Kit conditional knockout mouse (C57BL/6N−Kittm1c(EUCOMM)Mirow/J) with exon 4 flanked by LoxP sites. Kit tm1c homozygous Control animals had normal appearance, sex ratios, and reproductive success. Kit KO animals (using Pax2-Cre) exhibited hypopigmentation but normal sex and genotype ratios. Cerebellar Kit immunoreactivity was lost in Kit KO animals by both immunohistochemistry and western blot, while GAPDH and parvalbumin levels were equivalent.
evaluation: Claims C14, C19-C29, and C121-C123 describe the generation and validation of the Kit conditional knockout mouse. The validation is thorough, using multiple methods (immunohistochemistry, western blot) and appropriate controls (GAPDH, parvalbumin). The pigmentation phenotype provides gross confirmation of Pax2-Cre-mediated recombination. The preservation of Golgi cells (C25-C26) demonstrates specificity of the knockout.

result: Embryonic MLI Kit KO significantly altered the distribution of sIPSC event amplitudes and produced a significant decrease in sIPSC frequency (~50%) in PCs, with a less severe decrease in sIPSC amplitude and inhibitory charge. This reduced inhibition did not produce obvious impacts on spontaneous PC firing dynamics (membrane potential, membrane resistivity, action potential frequency, ISI, ISI CV2 were not significantly different), though there was some difference in the distribution of individual ISIs. The reduced sIPSC frequency was not associated with changes in MLI density, distribution, or molecular layer thickness.
evaluation: Claims C31-C37 are supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2. The statistical analyses are appropriate (KS test for distributions, t-tests for means). The sample sizes are adequate (29 Control vs 22 Kit KO cells for PC firing dynamics). The lack of changes in MLI density and distribution rules out gross anatomical defects as the cause of reduced inhibition.

result: MLI capacitance, input resistance, and spontaneous or evoked action potential frequency were not different between Control and Kit KO. Direct electrode stimulation in a paired-pulse paradigm evoked IPSCs of equivalent mean amplitude in PCs from Control and Kit KO conditions, with no difference in paired pulse ratio. These data suggest that electrical stimulation can produce IPSCs of similar amplitude and that release probability of individual synapses is unchanged between Control and Kit KO conditions.
evaluation: Claims C38-C42 are supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3. The interpretation that release probability is unchanged (C42) is reasonable based on the paired-pulse ratio data, though this is an inference. The normal MLI firing properties rule out presynaptic excitability defects.

result: The density and average size of GABAergic synapses onto PCs (triple-positive VGAT, gephyrin, and calbindin puncta) was not reduced by Kit KO. However, pinceau structures were preserved but smaller in Kit KO, with decreased Kv1.2 and PSD-95 immunoreactivity. Pinceaux size decreased by ~50% in Kit KO. These results suggest that Kit KO MLIs may have defects in physical and/or functional maturation of synapses onto PCs.
evaluation: Claims C43-C49 are supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4. The use of PSD-95 as a marker of pinceau size is validated by citation to Zhou et al., 2020 (C47). The sample sizes are adequate (26 Control vs 43 Kit KO pinceaux from 5 Control vs 8 Kit KO animals). The interpretation (C49) is reasonable given the anatomical and electrophysiological data.

result: In PCs of Kit KO, there was a significant ~50% reduction in the average frequency, but not amplitude, of mIPSCs. The frequency and amplitude of mEPSCs in PCs from Control and Kit KO did not differ. Mean mIPSC frequency and amplitude in MLIs was unchanged between Control and Kit KO. Therefore, embryonic MLI Kit KO was associated with a specific defect in the number or proportion of functional GABAergic synapses onto PCs.
evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 2K-M. The specificity of the effect (reduced mIPSC frequency in PCs but not mEPSC frequency in PCs or mIPSC frequency in MLIs) is a key finding. The interpretation (C53) is well-supported by the data. The predominant effect on frequency rather than amplitude suggests a presynaptic or synapse number phenotype.

result: Postnatal PC KL KO (using Pcp2-Cre) produced significant differences in the distribution of sIPSC event amplitudes and reduced the average sIPSC frequency, amplitude, and total inhibitory charge transfer in PCs, without changes to PC capacitance or membrane resistance. There was a substantial reduction in mIPSC frequency but not amplitude in PCs. The frequency and amplitude of mEPSCs in KL KO PCs were not different vs Controls. The per-animal average size or density of triple-positive VGAT/gephyrin/calbindin synaptic puncta and PSD-95+ pinceau area were not decreased. Thus, postnatal KL KO apparently reduced the proportion of functional GABAergic synapse sites upon PCs and specifically reduced synaptic GABAergic inhibition of PCs.
evaluation: Claims C54-C66 are supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3. The phenotype is similar to but more pronounced than the embryonic Kit KO phenotype. The statistical analyses are appropriate (KS tests, t-tests). The specificity for GABAergic synapses is demonstrated by the lack of effect on mEPSCs. The interpretation that the proportion of functional synapses is reduced (C60) is reasonable given the lack of change in synapse puncta density. The small differences in mIPSC and mEPSC amplitude distributions (C62-C64) are unlikely to account for the large decrease in mIPSC frequency (C65).

result: Recombination by Pcp2-Cre begins at ~P7, whereas Pax2-Cre recombination occurs at ~E15. The results suggest that continued expression of the KL-Kit dyad sustains inhibitory drive to PCs.
evaluation: Claims C67 and C68 are supported by citations to Barski et al., 2000 and Ohyama and Groves, 2004; Maricich and Herrup, 1999. The inference (C69) is reasonable given the comparison of embryonic Kit KO and postnatal KL KO results, though it would be strengthened by additional time-course experiments.

result: Sparse viral-mediated PC KL KO at P7, P18, or P56 reduced PC sIPSC frequency and inhibitory charge transferred. Conversely, KL overexpression (OX) in PCs increased sIPSC frequency, amplitude, and inhibitory charge transferred compared to nearby Control PCs. However, the relative local increase in inhibitory drive to KL OX PCs was not beyond the level of inhibition recorded in PCs from separate Sham animals, suggesting that the local gain in synaptic input to KL OX PCs appears to come at the expense of decreasing inhibition to nearby Control PCs.
evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The viral approach allows for temporal control and demonstrates that KL-Kit function is required throughout development and into adulthood. The KL OX experiment provides gain-of-function evidence. The interpretation (C74) is speculative but reasonable given the data showing that KL OX PCs have increased inhibition while adjacent Control PCs have decreased inhibition. However, the mechanism remains unclear and requires further investigation.

result: MLI number, distribution, action potential firing, and the density of GABAergic synaptic puncta onto PCs are all apparently normal in MLI Kit KO. These data suggest that while MLI axon terminals are present in Kit KO, they may be less functional. An increased failure rate between action potential generation and neurotransmitter release would be consistent with the normal firing frequency and synapse puncta density but decreased sIPSC and mIPSC frequency observed. Under the PPR paradigm, the apparently equivalent evoked responses may be due to direct stimulation of axon terminals and/or simultaneous recruitment of multiple MLIs. Kit KO most directly impacts the MLI:PC synapse, based on seemingly normal miniature events for parallel fiber:PC synapses (mEPSC in PC) and MLI:MLI (mIPSC in MLI) synapses.
evaluation: Claims C75-C79 are summary statements and interpretations by the authors based on their data. C75 is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, 3, and 4. C76 is a reasonable inference from the data. C77 and C78 are speculative interpretations to explain the observations, which is appropriate in a Discussion section. C79 is a well-supported conclusion based on the specificity of the electrophysiological effects.

result: Cerebellins and calsystenin impact multiple forms of synaptic input to PCs, making the specificity of KL-Kit for MLI:PC synapses a critical distinction. The residual inhibitory drive to PCs observed in MLI Kit KO or PC KL KO may come from PC axon collaterals, whose input might be preserved if KL-Kit functions primarily to mediate connectivity between different cell types. The histological analysis of synaptic puncta does not resolve between MLI:PC and PC:PC synapses, the relative balance of which may be altered by either KL or Kit manipulations.
evaluation: Claims C80 and C81 are supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2015 and Liu et al., 2022. C82 and C83 are speculative interpretations supported by citations to Chan-Palay, 1971; Larramendi and Lemkey-Johnston, 1970; Orduz and Llano, 2007; Witter et al., 2016. C84 is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation. C85 is a speculative interpretation. These claims appropriately identify limitations and alternative explanations.

result: PC KL OX may excessively potentiate MLI Kit to enhance MLI:MLI inhibition, reducing the inhibitory output surrounding MLIs can provide to control PCs. The KL-Kit axis, from embryonic development through young adulthood, can alter GABAergic drive to PCs. These results suggest that KL-Kit may be necessary to maintain, and perhaps capable of modulating, MLI:PC GABAergic inhibition in the adult cerebellum.
evaluation: Claim C87 is a speculative interpretation to explain the KL OX data. Claims C88 and C89 are conclusions drawn from the data showing effects of KL-Kit manipulation at multiple developmental time points (embryonic Kit KO, postnatal KL KO, and viral-mediated KL manipulation at P7, P18, and P56). These conclusions are well-supported by the data.

result: Each MLI has axon collaterals that can target multiple PCs, and each PC can receive input from multiple MLIs. Dynamics in the expression or shedding of KL may act through presynaptic Kit to tune the degree of convergent MLI:PC inhibitory drive. This would complement existing forms of modulation at the MLI:PC synapse, such as those dependent on PC-derived signaling molecules like endocannabinoids, secretin, and CR. The physiology of PCs and the structure of MLI:PC inhibition varies over zones such as those identified by Zebrin-II and PLCβ4.
evaluation: Claims C90 and C91 are established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry. C92 is a speculative interpretation by the authors. Claims C93-C95 are supported by citations to Kreitzer et al., 2002; Kreitzer and Regehr, 2001; Safo et al., 2006; Williams et al., 2012; Fuchs et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2020. C96 is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2014; Brochu et al., 1990; Leclerc et al., 1990; Sarna et al., 2006; Marzban et al., 2007. These claims provide context for the potential functional significance of KL-Kit signaling.

result: Kit is a receptor tyrosine kinase that can activate multiple downstream effectors, including Src family kinases, PLC, PI3K/mTOR, and the MAPK pathway, the latter two affiliated with synapse phenotypes and autism spectrum disorder. Trans-cellular interactions between KL and Kit may function in a kinase-independent, cell adhesion molecule modality. Adhesion molecules such as neurexins/neuroligins, dystrophin/dystroglycan, semaphorins, and neurofascins are important in the organization and maintenance of MLI:PC inhibition, with much of this understanding revealed by postsynaptic phenotypes involving cis- and trans interacting proteins that, via gephyrin, maintain the organization of PC GABAA receptors. MLI Kit or PC KL KO has a more predominant effect on mIPSC frequency than on amplitude, suggesting a presynaptic phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C97-C105 are supported by established knowledge and citations to the literature (Adachi et al., 1992; Tabone-Eglinger et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2022; Ango et al., 2004; Buttermore et al., 2012; Telley et al., 2016; Cioni et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2022). C106 is an inference drawn by the authors from their electrophysiology data. These claims provide context for potential molecular mechanisms and distinguish the KL-Kit phenotype from other synaptic adhesion molecules.

result: The authors have not observed overt cerebellar signs (i.e., ataxia) despite the reduced PC inhibition resulting from MLI Kit KO or PC KL KO, which is suspected to be due to compensation. Developmental ablation of functional GABAA channels in PCs does not produce overt motor signs, while adulthood ablation can. Behavioral phenotypes might be unmasked if KL or Kit KO is delayed until adulthood. Consistent with the interpretation that developmental compensation may be involved, the impact of postnatal PC KL KO on inhibitory drive to PCs is more pronounced than embryonic MLI Kit KO.
evaluation: Claim C107 is a direct observation by the authors. C108 is a speculative interpretation. C109 is supported by citation to Wisden et al., 2009. C110 is a speculative interpretation based on C109. C111 is an inference drawn from comparing the embryonic Kit KO and postnatal KL KO data. These claims appropriately acknowledge the lack of behavioral phenotypes and provide reasonable explanations.

result: MLI:PC GABAergic inhibition constrains granule cell-mediated PC dendritic excitation and gates the conversion of PC LTD to LTP at the PF-PC synapse in motor learning. KL or Kit KO may only reveal phenotypes in motor learning (or other cerebellar-plasticity dependent) behaviors. Global hypomorphs for KL or Kit have altered hippocampal neurophysiology and learning performance on a Water Maze task. Continuous expression of KL and Kit in specific neurons may reflect a role in the development (or maintenance) of synaptic function and in the plastic modulation of synaptic strength.
evaluation: Claim C112 is supported by citations to Bonnan et al., 2023; Gaffield et al., 2018. C113 is a speculative interpretation. C114 is supported by citations to Motro et al., 1996; Katafuchi et al., 2000; Kondo et al., 2002. C115 and C116 are speculative interpretations based on the authors' findings. These claims provide context for potential functional consequences and future directions.

result: KL-Kit regulates mammalian central synapse function, as demonstrated by impacts at the mouse GABAergic MLI:PC synapse. Kit and KL are expressed in diverse organisms and neuronal populations including glutamatergic neurons of the hippocampus, and neurons in olfactory bulb, basal forebrain, and brainstem. It is feasible that the synaptic phenotypes reported here reflect that KL-Kit is broadly capable of influencing connectivity.
evaluation: Claims C117 and C118 are conclusions drawn by the authors from their data. C119 is established knowledge about Kit and KL expression patterns. C120 is a speculative interpretation based on the widespread expression of Kit and KL. These claims appropriately summarize the main findings and suggest broader implications.
